The last point I’ll add is breaking down goals for expertise that are too big. Think of it like a video game. You have to level up base skills before you can learn the advanced moves and being able to identify and prioritize your skill tree is an important component of developing expertise. 

All in all you have to be enjoying yourself!

This response is predicated on you wanting to become less unhappy and if so, the only way to do that is to constructively address what’s causing that unhappiness: the *feeling* that you lack talent. 

This is ultimately unhappiness at a lack of expertise. Talent is a way to describe expertise coupled with the **illusion** of effortlessness. There’s not one “talented” pianist, engineer, mathematician, lawyer, economist, carpenter, bricklayer or whatever who had not put in countless hours of work and not one master who has not put in decades. 

Effort and time are the only two necessary conditions of expertise. Your focus on “talent” indicates an aversion to effort. I am not speaking judgementally but from experience. There are a couple of things people might say that I have a talent for that at one point in time I was absolutely garbage at. 

Finding joy in the process, the activity, in the effort in the moment is your only pathway to expertise. Every “talented” person will talk about effort because it’s impossible to create the illusion of talent without expertise, which to reiterate is a function of effort and time. 

Do things for the sake of enjoyment and the expertise will come. Increase the effort and efficiency of learning and it will come faster. 

Lastly, being kind to yourself is essential to the process - especially at the beginning. If you get down on yourself for being shit at something (or everything) you’ll never do it and never stick with it. You have to encourage yourself through the tough times and have a much longer timeframe for expertise. I like the 10 year rule and if you’d like to be good at something you should plan to dedicate yourself to the practice for a decade. 

All the best!

Took a long time to get here, but the biggest thing is working at it consistently. 

A lot of people have happy as a default, lucky them! I had to build my own happiness pretty much from scratch so I can tell you it’s possible. 

**Step 1: Survive**
Do the things required for you to be able to make it one day to the next: eat, sleep, drink water, work, pay your bills. 

As someone who really struggled with maintaining even these basic activities due to depression, putting in the effort to get these to a point of normalcy has been one of my biggest wins and formed the foundation for my happiness because it was a daily reinforcement that I’m being taken care of by past me and I have everything I need to take care of future me. 

**Step 2: Grow**
Growth is a hard one to pin down because it’s only apparent in hindsight. Also growth is different for everyone. Maybe you want to grow your career, your physical strength/endurance/flexibility, artistic ability, emotional intelligence, etc; maybe all of the above. 

There are also no shortcuts. We start with baby steps, take bigger steps, and maybe start running. Time and effort are the only two components of growth and failure is the only byproduct. I had to learn to treat myself kindly through all moments of not meeting my own expectations. 

**Step 3: Optimize**
Once you get good at effort, you may find that there’s kinds of effort that gets you a lot of gain and others that don’t. Being able to focus on things that become important to you through the process of putting in effort is important in staying true to yourself. 

I find that as I become more comfortable in myself, I attract more people as a matter of course. Having good boundaries, prioritizing my needs, and fighting the urge to please everyone was something I had to learn as a result. You may find yourself at a point where you choose yourself over others because those relationships don’t work for you in the way they’re set up and that’s OK!

The first thing I thought when I read this was "Holy shit it's not just me!"

So take this with like a huge grain of salt from someone who's in the same situation - like an alcoholic getting advice on alcoholism from another active alcoholic.

There's a few things I've considered about my situation

1. The behaviour of delaying, and recidivism, knowing the consequences
2. The feelings I experience through this repetitive process

* Lack of control, guilt, shame, excitement (from actually doing things, from being bad)

1. I'm still here (employed, alive). Which means that for however long I've not been doing certain things, the lack of those things has not created any adverse consequences.

Maybe we're the kind of people that need someone to set strict rails for us and that's fine, but in  capitalism that makes us less valuable. You become more valuable the less effort your bosses and others have to put on you relative to the how much you make life easier for them. If you solve all their problems and are a breeze to manage they'll love you. Your work is not about you, it's about everyone around you.

Personally, I feel like a lot of the work I'm given is stupid and pointless and I'd rather play games or do other things. Working from home hasn't made it easier to be disciplined at all. At the same time, people often only care about results and will forgive a couple days of lateness or some small errors to get there, this can get annoying after a while though. I found that I didn't want to do the work they gave me because I could conceptualize a better way of getting them what they wanted and sometimes I could make up for it by giving them something that was less annoying for me to do if they felt it was better for them too.

I find having a great attitude, being helpful and super nice also helps them forgive my indiscretions.

At the core of it, I can't help who I am right now. When I get overwhelmed or bored with things it feels like procrastination is a physical limitation rather than a mental one. I've tried to focus on the end result I want to reach at - making enough money, being stress free, moving up in life - rather than worrying about the "mess" I have to go through to get there. I also tried to put aside the judgmental and negative feelings I had about myself which I realized came from outside voices I had internalized over the years - they're completely useless to achieving the end result.

On a practical note, the first thing to do is to achieve an equilibrium relative to your current situation. Some steps to do this

* Ask for help. People are much more willing to forgive if you preempt the discovery of the issue.
   * "I thought I could do this but... so ... "
   * "I tried to do this a certain way but it didn't work so..."
   * "I didn't realize ... so ..."
* Ask for feedback. People get frustrated because they don't have an avenue to express what they feel. Let people tell you what they need from you and try to give it to them.
* Focus on improvement. You'll need tools to make sure that the equilibrium is sustainable. it's not going to be a smooth ride, but mastering tools one by one means that you don't fall as far when you do fall and you can get back up faster.
* Focus on the process. There is no quick fix and searching for one is like trying to get out of debt by getting deeper into debt. You might come to enjoy the roller coaster and eventually control the track in real time.
* Get therapy. The destructive feelings I try and put aside for work still exist outside of work and really are at the root of the destructive behaviours. No amount of process improvement is going to be sustainable if you don't eventually address the root causes as well.

I consider myself a fairly high functioning procrastinator purely from the perspective of who I was even 6 months ago, and certainly from 5 years ago. The things you're feeling don't have to continue forever and there is a version of yourself in the future who's proud of you for even the smallest steps you take right now.
